questions.question: Let $x$ and $y$ be real numbers such that $50\left(\dfrac{2x}{1+3i} - \dfrac{y}{1-2i}\right) = 31 + 17i$, $i = \sqrt{-1}$. Then the value of $10(x - 3y)$ is :
questions.solution:
Given the equation:

$50\left(\dfrac{2x}{1+3i} - \dfrac{y}{1-2i}\right) = 31 + 17i$

Rationalizing the denominators inside the parentheses:

$\dfrac{2x}{1+3i} = \dfrac{2x(1-3i)}{(1+3i)(1-3i)} = \dfrac{2x(1-3i)}{1^2 + 3^2} = \dfrac{2x(1-3i)}{10} = \dfrac{x(1-3i)}{5}$

$\dfrac{y}{1-2i} = \dfrac{y(1+2i)}{(1-2i)(1+2i)} = \dfrac{y(1+2i)}{1^2 + 2^2} = \dfrac{y(1+2i)}{5}$

Substituting these back into the given equation:

$50\left(\dfrac{x(1-3i)}{5} - \dfrac{y(1+2i)}{5}\right) = 31 + 17i$

$10(x(1-3i) - y(1+2i)) = 31 + 17i$

$10(x - y) - 10i(3x + 2y) = 31 + 17i$

Equating the real and imaginary parts on both sides:

$10(x - y) = 31 \Rightarrow 10x - 10y = 31$

$-10(3x + 2y) = 17 \Rightarrow -30x - 20y = 17$

Multiplying the first equation by $3$ gives:

$30x - 30y = 93$

Adding this to the second equation:

$(-30x - 20y) + (30x - 30y) = 17 + 93$

$-50y = 110 \Rightarrow y = -\dfrac{11}{5}$

Substituting $y = -\dfrac{11}{5}$ into $10x - 10y = 31$:

$10x - 10\left(-\dfrac{11}{5}\right) = 31$

$10x + 22 = 31 \Rightarrow 10x = 9 \Rightarrow x = \dfrac{9}{10}$

Now, finding the value of $10(x - 3y)$:

$10(x - 3y) = 10x - 30y = 10\left(\dfrac{9}{10}\right) - 30\left(-\dfrac{11}{5}\right)$

$10(x - 3y) = 9 + 66 = 75$

Answer: $75$

Then $\mathop{∑}_{\left(\alpha, \beta\right) \in S}\left(i{Z}_{\alpha\beta} + \dfrac{1}{i\overset{¯}{Z}\alpha\beta}\right)$ is equal to
questions.solution:
Given $\pi < \alpha, \beta < 2\pi$

$\dfrac{1 - isin\alpha}{1 + i\left(2sin\alpha\right)}$ is purely imaginary

$⇒ \dfrac{\left(1 - isin\alpha\right)\left(1 - i\left(2sin\alpha\right)\right)}{1 + 4{sin}^{2}\alpha}$ is purely imaginary

$⇒ \dfrac{1 - 2{sin}^{2}\alpha}{1 + 4{sin}^{2}\alpha} = 0$

$⇒ {sin}^{2}\alpha = \dfrac{1}{2}$

$⇒ \alpha = \left\{\dfrac{5\pi}{4}, \dfrac{7\pi}{4}\right\}$

Also $\dfrac{1 + icos\beta}{1 + i\left(- 2cos\beta\right)}$ is purely real

$⇒ \dfrac{\left(1 + icos\beta\right)\left(1 + 2icos\beta\right)}{1 + 4{cos}^{2}\beta}$ is purely real

$⇒ 3cos\beta = 0$

$⇒ \beta = \dfrac{3\pi}{2}$

Now ${Z}_{\alpha\beta} = sin2\alpha + icos2\beta$

$⇒ {Z}_{\alpha\beta} = sin\dfrac{5\pi}{2} + icos3\pi = 1 - i$

or ${Z}_{\alpha\beta} = sin\dfrac{7\pi}{2} + icos3\pi = - 1 - i$

$\mathop{∑}_{\left(\alpha, \beta\right) \in S}\left(i{Z}_{\alpha\beta} + \dfrac{1}{i\overset{¯}{Z}\alpha\beta}\right)$$= \left[i\left(1 - i\right) + \dfrac{1}{i\left(1 + i\right)}\right] + \left[i\left(- 1 - i\right) + \dfrac{1}{i\left(- 1 + i\right)}\right]$

$= \left[i + 1 - \dfrac{i\left(1 - i\right)}{2}\right] + \left[- i + 1 + \dfrac{i\left(1 + i\right)}{2}\right]$

$= 2 - 1 = 1$

questions.question: Let $S = \left\{z \in \mathbb{C} - { i, 2i } : \dfrac{{z}^{2} + 8iz - 15}{{z}^{2} - 3iz - 2} \in \mathbb{R}\right\}$. $\alpha - \dfrac{13}{11}i \in S, \alpha \in \mathbb{R} - { 0 }$, then $242{α}^{2}$ is equal to
questions.solution:
Put $z = x + iy$ in the given expression and equate the imaginary part to zero.

$⇒ \dfrac{{z}^{2} + 8iz - 15}{{z}^{2} - 3iz - 2} = \dfrac{\left(x + iy\right)2 + 8i\left(x + iy\right) - 15}{\left(x + iy\right)2 - 3i\left(x + iy\right) - 2}$

$= \dfrac{{x}^{2} - {y}^{2} - 8y - 15 + i\left(2xy + 8x\right)}{{x}^{2} - {y}^{2} + 3y - 2 + i\left(2xy - 3x\right)}$

$= \dfrac{{x}^{2} - {y}^{2} - 8y - 15 + i\left(2xy + 8x\right)}{{x}^{2} - {y}^{2} + 3y - 2 + i\left(2xy - 3x\right)} \times \left({x}^{2} - {y}^{2} + 3y - 2 - i\left(2xy - 3x\right)\right)\left({x}^{2} - {y}^{2} + 3y - 2 - i\left(2xy - 3x\right)\right)$

$= \dfrac{\left({x}^{2} - {y}^{2} - 8y - 15\right)\left({x}^{2} - {y}^{2} + 3y - 2\right) + \left(2xy + 8x\right)\left(2xy - 3x\right) + i\left(2xy + 8x\right)\left({x}^{2} - {y}^{2} + 3y - 2\right) - i\left(2xy - 3x\right)\left({x}^{2} - {y}^{2} - 8y - 15\right)}{\left({x}^{2} - {y}^{2} + 3y - 2\right)2 - \left(2xy - 3x\right)2}$

But $Im\left(\dfrac{{z}^{2} + 8iz - 15}{{z}^{2} - 3iz - 2}\right) = 0$,

$⇒ - \left({x}^{2} - {y}^{2} - 8y - 15\right)\left(2xy - 3x\right) + \left(2xy + 8x\right)\left({x}^{2} - {y}^{2} + 3y - 2\right) = 0$

$⇒ \left({x}^{2} - {y}^{2}\right)\left(2xy + 8x - 2xy + 3x\right) + \left(8y + 15\right)\left(2xy - 3x\right) + \left(2xy + 8x\right)\left(3y - 2\right) = 0$

$⇒ 11{x}^{3} - 11x{y}^{2} + 16x{y}^{2} - 24xy + 30xy - 45x + 6x{y}^{2} - 4xy + 24xy - 16x = 0$

$⇒ 11{x}^{3} + 11x{y}^{2} + 26xy - 61x = 0$

$⇒ 11{x}^{2} + 11{y}^{2} + 26y - 61 = 0$

$∵ \alpha \ne 0$

So, put $y = - \dfrac{13}{11}$, $x = \alpha$
$11{α}^{2} + 11 \cdot \dfrac{132}{112} - 26 \cdot \dfrac{13}{11} - 61 = 0$
$⇒ 121{α}^{2} = 840$

$⇒ 242{α}^{2} = 1680$

Hence this is the required answer.

(S1) : The set $\left\{\mathrm{z} \in \mathbb{C}-\{-\mathrm{i}\}:|\mathrm{z}|=1\right.$ and $\frac{\mathrm{z}-\mathrm{i}}{\mathrm{z}+\mathrm{i}}$ is purely real} contains exactly two elements, and (S2) : The set $\left\{\mathrm{z} \in \mathbb{C}-\{-1\}:|\mathrm{z}|=1\right.$ and $\frac{\mathrm{z}-1}{\mathrm{z}+1}$ is purely imaginary contains infinitely many elements.
questions.question:
Among the statements
(S1) : The set $\left\{\mathrm{z} \in \mathbb{C}-\{-\mathrm{i}\}:|\mathrm{z}|=1\right.$ and $\frac{\mathrm{z}-\mathrm{i}}{\mathrm{z}+\mathrm{i}}$ is purely real} contains exactly two elements, and (S2) : The set $\left\{\mathrm{z} \in \mathbb{C}-\{-1\}:|\mathrm{z}|=1\right.$ and $\frac{\mathrm{z}-1}{\mathrm{z}+1}$ is purely imaginary contains infinitely many elements.
questions.solution: $\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{S}_1:|\mathrm{z}|=1, \frac{\mathrm{z}-\mathrm{i}}{\mathrm{z}+\mathrm{i}}=\frac{\overline{\mathrm{z}}+\mathrm{i}}{\overline{\mathrm{z}}-\mathrm{i}} \\ & \Rightarrow(\mathrm{z}-\mathrm{i})(\overline{\mathrm{z}}-\mathrm{i})=(\mathrm{z}+\mathrm{i})(\overline{\mathrm{z}}+\mathrm{i}) \\ & |\mathrm{z}|^2-\mathrm{i}(\mathrm{z}+\overline{\mathrm{z}})-1=|\mathrm{z}|^2+\mathrm{i}(\mathrm{z}+\overline{\mathrm{z}})-1 \\ & \mathrm{i}(\mathrm{z}+\overline{\mathrm{z}})=0 \\ & \mathrm{z}+\overline{\mathrm{z}}=2 \cos \theta=0 \Rightarrow \cos \theta=0 \\ & \mathrm{z}=0+0 \mathrm{i},|\mathrm{z}| \neq 1 \\ & \mathrm{~S}_1: \frac{\mathrm{z}-1}{\mathrm{z}+1}+\frac{\overline{\mathrm{z}}-1}{\overline{\mathrm{z}}+1}=0 \\ & (\mathrm{z}-1)(\overline{\mathrm{z}}+1)+(\mathrm{z}+1)(\overline{\mathrm{z}}-1)=0 \\ & \Rightarrow|\mathrm{z}|^2+(\mathrm{z}-\overline{\mathrm{z}})-1+|\mathrm{z}|^2+(\mathrm{z}-\overline{\mathrm{z}})-1=0 \\ & |\mathrm{z}|^2=1\end{aligned}$

questions.question: If $\alpha$ denotes the number of solutions of $\left|1 - i\right|x = {2}^{x}$ and $\beta = \left(\left|z\right|arg\left(z\right)\right)$, where $z = \dfrac{π}{4}\left(1 + i\right)4\left(\dfrac{1 - \sqrt{\pi} \cdot i}{\sqrt{\pi} + i} + \dfrac{\sqrt{\pi} - i}{1 + \sqrt{\pi} \cdot i}\right)$, $i = \sqrt{- 1}$, then the distance of the point $\left(\alpha, \beta\right)$ from the line $4x - 3y = 7$ is ______
questions.solution:
Given,

$\left|1 - i\right|x = {2}^{x}$

$⇒ \left(\sqrt{2}\right)x = {2}^{x}$

$⇒ x = 0$

Hence, the number of solutions will be one, so $\alpha = 1$

Now, solving

$z = \dfrac{π}{4}\left(1 + i\right)4\left(\dfrac{1 - \sqrt{\pi} \cdot i}{\sqrt{\pi} + i} + \dfrac{\sqrt{\pi} - i}{1 + \sqrt{\pi} \cdot i}\right)$

$⇒ z = \dfrac{π}{4}\left(1 + i\right)4\left[\dfrac{\sqrt{\pi} - \pii - i - \sqrt{\pi}}{\pi + 1} + \dfrac{\sqrt{\pi} - i - \pii - \sqrt{\pi}}{1 + \pi}\right]$

$⇒ z = \dfrac{π}{4}\left(1 + i\right)4\left[\dfrac{- 2\pii - 2i}{\pi + 1}\right]$

$⇒ z = \dfrac{\pii}{2}\left(1 + i\right)4$

$⇒ z = - \dfrac{\pii}{2}\left(1 + 4i + 6{i}^{2} + 4{i}^{3} + 1\right)$

$⇒ z = 2\pii$

So, $arg\left(z\right) = \dfrac{π}{2}$

$⇒ \beta = \left|z\right|arg\left(z\right) = \dfrac{2\pi}{\dfrac{π}{2}} = 4$

Hence, the distance from $\left(\alpha, \beta\right) ≡ \left(1, 4\right)$ to $4x - 3y = 7$ will be $\left|\dfrac{4 - 3 \times 4 - 7}{{4}^{2} + {3}^{2}}\right| = \dfrac{15}{5} = 3$

Hence,

Now, ${x}^{2} + \sqrt{6}x + 3 = 0$ has roots $\alpha \text{ and } \beta$

So, $x = \dfrac{- \sqrt{6} \pm \sqrt{- 6}}{2}$

$⇒ x = \sqrt{6}\left(\dfrac{- 1 \pm i}{2}\right)$

$⇒ x = \sqrt{3}\left(\dfrac{- 1 \pm i}{2}\right)$

$\Rightarrow y^2=\frac{3}{64}$.
So $|z|^2=\frac{1}{64}+\frac{3}{64}=\frac{1}{16}$.
$\sum|z|^2=0+\frac{1}{16}+\frac{1}{16}+\frac{1}{16}=\frac{3}{16}$

questions.question: Let $S=\{z \in \mathbb{C}: z^2+4z+16=0\}$. Then $\sum_{z \in S}|z+\sqrt{3}i|^2$ is equal to:

Given the equation $z^2 + 4z + 16 = 0$, we find its roots using the quadratic formula:

$z = \dfrac{-4 \pm \sqrt{16 - 64}}{2} = \dfrac{-4 \pm \sqrt{-48}}{2} = -2 \pm 2\sqrt{3}i$

The set $S$ contains two complex numbers: $z_1 = -2 + 2\sqrt{3}i$ and $z_2 = -2 - 2\sqrt{3}i$.

We need to evaluate the sum $\sum_{z \in S} |z + \sqrt{3}i|^2$, which is $|z_1 + \sqrt{3}i|^2 + |z_2 + \sqrt{3}i|^2$.

For $z_1 = -2 + 2\sqrt{3}i$:

$|-2 + 3\sqrt{3}i|^2 = (-2)^2 + (3\sqrt{3})^2 = 4 + 27 = 31$

$|-2 - \sqrt{3}i|^2 = (-2)^2 + (-\sqrt{3})^2 = 4 + 3 = 7$

Adding these values together:

$\sum_{z \in S} |z + \sqrt{3}i|^2 = 31 + 7 = 38$

Answer: $38$

questions.question: Let $S = \{z \in \mathbb{C} : z^2 + \sqrt{6}\,iz - 3 = 0\}$. Then $\sum\limits_{z \in S} z^8$ is equal to :
questions.solution:
Given equation is $z^2 + \sqrt{6}iz - 3 = 0$.

Rearranging the terms, we get $z^2 - 3 = -\sqrt{6}iz$.

Squaring both sides, we obtain:

$(z^2 - 3)^2 = (-\sqrt{6}iz)^2$

$z^4 - 6z^2 + 9 = -6z^2$

$z^4 + 9 = 0$

$z^4 = -9$

Squaring again, we get:

$(z^4)^2 = (-9)^2$

$z^8 = 81$

Since the given equation is a quadratic in $z$, it has two roots, say $z_1$ and $z_2$.

The discriminant of the quadratic equation is $\Delta = (\sqrt{6}i)^2 - 4(1)(-3) = -6 + 12 = 6 \neq 0$, which means the roots are distinct.

Thus, the set $S$ contains two distinct elements $z_1$ and $z_2$.

For each root, $z^8 = 81$.

Therefore, $\sum\limits_{z \in S} z^8 = z_1^8 + z_2^8 = 81 + 81 = 162$.

Answer: $162$

Fourth powers: $(2)^4 = 16$, $(-1)^4 = 1$.
For $n = 1$ to $25$: 8 multiples of 3 contribute $8 \times 16 = 128$, remaining 17 terms contribute $17 \times 1 = 17$.
Total $= 128 + 17 = 145$.

$∴ arg\left(\dfrac{2{z}_{2}}{3{z}_{1}}\right) = - \theta$

Also, we know that a complex number $w$ can be expressed as $w = \left|w\right|\left(cos\alpha + isin\alpha\right),$ where $\alpha$ is the argument of the complex number.

questions.question: Let $z \in C$ be such that $\left|z\right| < 1 .$ If $\omega = \dfrac{5 + 3z}{5\left(1 - z\right)},$ then:
questions.solution:
Given $\left|z\right| < 1$ and $\omega = \dfrac{5 + 3z}{5\left(1 - z\right)}$

$⇒ 5\omega\left(1 - z\right) = 5 + 3z$

$⇒ 5\omega - 5\omegaz = 5 + 3z$

$⇒ z = \dfrac{5\omega - 5}{3 + 5\omega}$

Using the given condition $\left|z\right| = 5\left|\dfrac{\omega - 1}{3 + 5\omega}\right| < 1$


$⇒ 5\left|\omega - 1\right| < \left|3 + 5\omega\right|$

$⇒ 5\left|\omega - 1\right| < 5\left|\omega + \dfrac{3}{5}\right|$

$⇒ \left|\omega - 1\right| < \left|\omega - \left(- \dfrac{3}{5}\right)\right|$

We know that the locus of a complex number ${z}_{1}$ satisfying $\left|{z}_{1} - a\right| = \left|{z}_{2} - b\right|$ is the perpendicular bisector of the line segment joining the points $a$ and $b .$

Hence, the locus of the point $\omega$ satisfying $\left|\omega - 1\right| = \left|\omega - \left(- \dfrac{3}{5}\right)\right|$ is the line $x = \dfrac{1 - \dfrac{3}{5}}{2} = \dfrac{1}{5}$

Hence, $Re\left(\omega\right) > \dfrac{1}{5}$

$⇒ 5Re\left(\omega\right) > 1 .$
